# Executive summary

This report describes calendar-month patterns in the unannualized
two-observation Yang–Zhang daily-volatility target for LSEG Workspace
`GCc1`, a generic COMEX gold futures series. The tracked prepared dataset
contains 3,801 valid targets from 2010-01-06 through 2026-11-10. We summarize
the target by month of year across all available years and separately by
individual calendar year-month. The tables also distinguish training and
previously examined test samples.

Across all valid observations, mean volatility is highest in March
(0.00899) and lowest in July (0.00694). This is a descriptive difference,
not evidence of a stable seasonal effect: the sample spans changing market
regimes, the Yang–Zhang target windows overlap, and no seasonality hypothesis
test is performed.

# Data and method

The input is
`data/processed/stage2_yz_selected/GCc1_yang_zhang_volatility.csv`.
It contains daily OHLC-derived Yang–Zhang variance and its square-root
volatility target, plus the chronological `train`/`test` split. The target is
not annualized. Rows with incomplete OHLC windows have missing targets and
are excluded; no prices or target values are imputed.

For the month-of-year summary, each valid target is grouped by its calendar
month number, pooling years. For the calendar-month summary, observations are
grouped by year and month. Both tables provide all-sample, training-only, and
test-only rows. Statistics are target count, year coverage, mean, median,
sample standard deviation, and the 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles.

The month-of-year summary is useful for describing the sample but does not
adjust for the long-run evolution in volatility, other market conditions,
missing bars, or repeated testing. A calendar pattern cannot be interpreted
as a causal effect. The chronological test segment has already informed
earlier model exploration and is not an untouched validation sample.

# Month-of-year summaries

The table below reports means, medians, counts, and 90th percentiles for the
full sample. The complete statistics, including training and test subsets,
are available in the linked machine-readable summary.

```{r}
months <- read.csv("yang-zhang-calendar-data/month_of_year_summary.csv")
all_months <- subset(months, sample == "all")
month_table <- data.frame(
  Month = all_months$month_name,
  Targets = all_months$n_targets,
  Years = all_months$n_years,
  Mean = sprintf("%.5f", all_months$mean_daily_volatility),
  Median = sprintf("%.5f", all_months$median_daily_volatility),
  `90th percentile` = sprintf("%.5f", all_months$q90_daily_volatility),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(month_table, format = "pipe", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

March has the largest full-sample mean, while July has the smallest. These
monthly group means pool observations over many years; differences can be
driven by a small number of high-volatility episodes or by shifts in the
overall volatility distribution.

![Mean and median by calendar month, and mean by individual calendar
month.](yang-zhang-calendar-data/calendar_month_summaries.png)

# Calendar year-month view

The year-month series makes changes in the level of volatility over time
visible alongside the month-of-year grouping. It is not a forecast and does
not isolate a recurring month effect. The individual year-month statistics
are provided in the
[calendar-month CSV](yang-zhang-calendar-data/calendar_month_summary.csv);
the month-of-year table, including training and test splits, is provided in
the [month-of-year CSV](yang-zhang-calendar-data/month_of_year_summary.csv).

# Reproducibility

From the repository root, regenerate the summary tables, figure, and
input-hash manifest, then render this report:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/analyze_yang_zhang_calendar.py \
  --output-dir reports/yang-zhang-calendar-data
quarto render reports/yang-zhang-calendar.qmd
```

The generator records the input SHA-256, sample dates, grouping definitions,
and output paths in
[`yang-zhang-calendar-data/manifest.json`](yang-zhang-calendar-data/manifest.json).
The input source is the prepared target file above; data-source access and
Yang–Zhang target construction are described in the project
[`README`](../README.md) and
[`reproduction guide`](../REPRODUCE.md).
